A new screen fills: a star field, sharp and crowded, with one bright point dead center and a small green crosshair sitting a hair to its left.

"There. That's a standard star. We know exactly how bright it is, so we point at it and lie to the telescope about where it is. Then we see how far the lie moved it." She broke one in half and held it out to you without a word.

It was too hot to hold properly. The crust cracked, the inside was soft and steaming, and the smell of it was the whole street at six in the morning and none of the people in it yet.

"Now you know," Noor said, and blew on her fingers. She glanced at the window, where the sky was still black. "Abu Samir will be here in forty minutes and he will complain it's too hot. Thirty years, every day, and every day too hot." She started loading the tray into a wide flat basket. "He's not wrong. It is too hot. That's the point."

I hang the gown by the door, sit down on the costume trunk in the corner, and watch the room.

Reply:
The room kept moving around you. A dresser ironed a shirt collar flat with quick, angry strokes. Two wigs sat on their blocks like patient heads, and a girl brushed one of them with long, even pulls. From the far corner came the dry, insistent clatter of a sewing machine. Somewhere above, the orchestra was tuning, a scattered field of notes that never quite became a chord.

Lucia crossed to the wall of drawers, pulled one open, and took out a card of silver hooks. She checked the gown once more on her way past, touched the hem with two fingers, and seemed satisfied.

Then she noticed you on the trunk.

"You're sitting," she said. It wasn't an accusation. She looked at the spool still in your hand, the red silk, and something in her face shifted, small, almost hidden.

"Keep that," she said. "Red silk. It matches the Bellini gown. If a stitch goes in act one, you'll be the one who has it." She turned back to the drawers. "First rule of this room. Never stand empty-handed on opening night. Second rule. Never sit down unless you can hear the whole room from where you're sitting. Can you hear it?"

The iron hissed. The wigs turned. The tuning above went on and on, and under all of it, faint, someone was laughing in the corridor.

The couch gave a little under you, and the right side held. Wren watched you settle in with the box on your knees, and something in her face eased, the way people look when a guest stops standing around being polite.

"You brought donuts to a radio station at two in the morning," she said. "That's either very kind or you're wanted by the law."

She turned back to the desk, and the two of you sat with the music. The song with strings finished, and she crossfaded into something slower, brushed drums and a man singing low, the kind of thing that sounded like it had been recorded in a room with bad wiring and good intentions. She kept her hand on the fader the whole way through the transition, riding it like a boat.

"Okay," she said when it was steady. "Here's the deal with this shift. I talk for about ninety seconds every fifteen minutes, and the rest of the time I'm just — here. So you don't have to make conversation. A lot of people think they do. They sit on that couch and narrate my own show back to me. It's exhausting."

She swiveled her chair halfway around to face you, one elbow on the armrest, and nodded at the box.

"So. What kind."

I sit back in the cane chair with my tea and watch the rain over the slopes.

Reply:
Ravi watches you taste, and something in his shoulders eases when you don't reach for the sugar. He takes his own sip, holding it a moment before he swallows.

"Good," he says, half to himself. "That's the lower slope, then. You can hear it in the cup." The cup goes back on its saucer, and one finger taps twice against the cane armrest. "You know, most buyers who come here want to talk about the factory, the numbers, the price per kilo. You sat down and looked at the rain. That is a good sign in a man."

The rain eases for a moment, then redoubles, and a small river runs down the gravel path toward the factory. Ravi leans forward to watch it, his elbows on his knees.

"Tomorrow, if the weather lifts, I'll take you up to the top field. Two thousand meters. On a clear day you can see the whole valley, and if you turn around, the Western Ghats going blue into the haze. The leaf up there is slow and small and bitter, and it makes the best tea on the estate." He glances at you sideways. "The buyers who only sit in the bungalow never see it. They taste it in a cup and think they know it."

The pot comes around again, both cups topped up without a word asked or given, and he leans back into the chair as the rain hammers overhead.

"Tell me something," he says. "Where I am from, the rain is either a blessing or a curse, and we argue about which all day. Where you are from — what is rain to you?"
